# Model Comparison -- deliverable 3

*Auto-generated by `src/report.py` (`full` dataset). Evaluated on held-out test
wafers, ELIGIBLE dies only (`old_label == 0`). 32,598 dies, 1,380
new failures (4.23%).*

## Model A -> B: does the block signal help?

| metric | Model A | Model B (pooling) | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| AUC-PR | 0.5476 | 0.5859 | **+0.0383** (+7.0%) |
| F1 (fail) | 0.5214 | 0.5491 | +0.0277 |
| recall | 0.4413 | 0.4029 | -0.0384 |
| precision | 0.6370 | 0.8620 | +0.2250 |

**Block-level data HELPS.**
A and B use the identical estimator and hyper-parameters; B differs only by the block
feature columns, so this delta measures the *data*, not two modelling choices.

## Tier 1 vs Tier 2: pooling or a learned encoder?

| architecture | AUC-PR | F1 |
|---|---|---|
| statistical pooling (25 features) | 0.5859 | 0.5491 |
| gated attention-MIL, late fusion | 0.5401 | 0.5164 |

**Winner: statistical pooling** (0.0458 AUC-PR).
We tested a learned encoder against statistical pooling and pooling won. That is a real finding, not a failure -- the PS asks for improvement *or lack thereof*. The MIL branch is retained for its attention weights, which give Model B a block interpretability artifact that pooling cannot provide.

## Versus the incumbent

Best incumbent method: **NNR (k=8)** at AUC-PR 0.0734.
Model B reaches 0.5859 --
**8.0x** better.

DPAT and GDBN assume univariate Gaussian parameter distributions. Recon Q5 measured a
median Cohen's d of ~0.14 across the 500 parametrics, so there is no single parameter for
a univariate rule to threshold on. That is the published critique of DPAT at advanced
nodes, reproduced here on our own data.

## Calibration and uncertainty

| | raw | isotonic-calibrated |
|---|---|---|
| Brier score | 0.0576 | 0.0244 |
| Expected calibration error | 0.1254 | 0.0027 |

### Per-die uncertainty

| method | mean interval width | band coverage |
|---|---|---|
| Venn-ABERS (IVAP) | 0.00134 | 0.10 |
| Bootstrap over the calibration set | 0.01109 | 0.90 |

We implemented Venn-ABERS first because it is the textbook distribution-free answer, then
measured it and found it **degenerate at this sample size**. IVAP's width shrinks as
O(1/n): with a 36,672-die calibration set the two isotonic fits differ by one point
in 36,672, so the interval collapses to ~0.0013 wide and brackets
the observed rate in only 10% of risk bands. It answers "how much
could one more observation move this estimate", which is not the question.

Resampling the calibration set answers the right question -- how much do we actually know
about this die's risk -- and its intervals bracket the observed failure rate in
**90%** of bands. We report both, and ship the bootstrap interval.
